text:
Upgraded from 2020 Model 3 (which I loved to death and couldn't even imagine how it could ever be improved aside from body/trim issues) => 2024 Model 3 LR few days ago. Oh boy, the difference is like switching from Camry to BMW 3. The overall heft, the way doors open/close, overall trim, handling, mood lights, no-stalk driving, backseat screen, ventilated seats, improved struts, etc., all make it feel like a completely different class of car. Highly recommend.

The 1 and only negative is that it feels a bit heavier - what I liked the most about my 2020 Model 3 was that for a very heavy car it felt so light and handling overall felt so effortless like a work of art. 2024 Model 3 LR on the other hand feels a bit more like a hefty luxury car with, and it leads to more physical exertion when handling.

text:
For an electric car that simply designed to make you go from point A to point B the performance doesn’t make sense to me.
Speed and acceleration is fun in a fast gas car. I’ve driven a plaid and a model 3 performance. Both those cars are incredibly quick, but the thrill is not the same compared to a gasoline engine, putting down those numbers.
It’s like cooking a steak, you could put that steak in a microwave to cook it and cook it quick. Or you could put that steak on a grill and it’ll take longer to cook, but it’ll taste a lot better and it’s more fun to grill. At the end of the day you end up with two cooked steaks.
I just personally would rather have an electric car that is adequate all the way around but gets 500 miles of range. If I wanna really exhilarating driving experience, I’ll get a Mustang GT 350 or a ZL1 Camaro.

author: @jmel1746
text:
Yeah!!! The embargo is lifted and we can see this car...Finally! I must add that you missed perhaps THE most exciting thing about this car = The new adaptive suspension. Usually there's a tradeoff dilemma for engineers - to make it daily/liveable, meaning too soft for sporty driving or race car harsh wherein potholes, heaves, asphalt patches, expansion joints and speedbumps jar your 
teeth. All the best cars from Germany any and even Cadillac ( MRC or Magnetic Ride Control ) offer adaptive damping that assesses road conditions, speed and turning force to provide accurate compliance for the situation at hand. This system is automatic or user configurable as well, so have at it as you please. Track mode v.3 is an upgrade too with new tweaks. The new wheels are lighter, too.

The suspension has new geometry and the brake pads , while not carbon ceramic, are new and improved over the last gen Performance 3. It would be nice, Elon, to have some new, differentiating colors other than the same six choices you've offered for the last 6 years as seen on millions of other Teslas. 

The seats look amazing yet I agree those steering wheel buttons need to have a tactile click. Its not a deal-breaker for me, but no stalks and no gear shifter are weird. I know there's Auto Drive like in the Plaid and people say it works well, so maybe that would make up for that omission...to me.

The Ioniq5N is a wagon and the looks don't do it for me. Its also slower and over $70,000.. The fake transmission and phoney engine noises are controversial. In my brain, when manufacturers create fake engine noises for EVs ( hello Porsche ) they lose me. Its like fake news - Intellectually, I know it's BS. Some OEMs cut the gears slightly different in their sporty EVs which creates a true, mechanical sound that is pleasing and communicates sensations of speedier motation.

All-in, I'm stoked to drive it and may trade in my 2018 Long Range. Next comes the price. If it's signicantly less than a Hyundai N or BMW, it'll be a no-brainer. Being the most American car you can buy also helps. A new S Plaid still tops $90,000 with wheels and paint. Maybe a used Plaid? Love the hatch but its a big car.....

Thank you for making this video and I hope you can give it a go on the track soon!

text:
Bought a Model 3 Performance in early 2019, owned one for 5yrs and had a great experience.  I find the prospect of the ‘all new Model 3’ incredibly boring.  While I like the upgrades and exterior refresh, the lack of driver screen remains lame on the 3 and Y, Tesla customer service is dire and creaking due to the rapid expansion of the company, and the Model 3 is super common everywhere now due to such cheap versions being available.  It’s relatively much cheaper now than when I got mine, which makes it much less exclusive, rare or desirable to me.  

Conclusion: I am bored of Tesla, the S and X are boring to me.  I picked up a 2022 Hummer EV with 4000mi on it, incredibly vehicle and pick up truck, an absolutely beast.  GM have completely nailed it and with supercharger network access now too, it was absolutely the right move for me.  Very happy with something higher end, rarer, more luxurious and people across the board stop me to rave about this vehicle.  GM did an incredible job with the Hummer EV, and it bodes well for their next gen EV’s elsewhere in the company.

text:
@Nickbaldeagle02 Good question.  Insurance can be a problem.  My insurance on my 2023 Model 3 is about the same as it was on my 2019 Honda Passport.  $500 every six months.  Just had to shop around a little.  I assume my insurance for this would be slightly more.

I had Geico when I first bought it and when I tried to add my Model 3 they quoted me $1600 every six months ON TOP OF what I was already paying.  State Farm quoted me $2400 every six months for just my Model 3.  I ended up with Progressive and it was actually only $400 for the first six months with a discount before going up to what it is now.  

I actually used Tesla insurance for a few months and that was even cheaper, ~$50-$60/mo, but I didn't like how restrictive it is and felt like I was getting penalized unfairly for certain things.

I think a lot of people don't shop around much, they just go with what they know.  I know I've been pretty bad about that in the past.  For example long ago I had Nationwide just because I'd had them since I got my license and one day just asked my agent and she was able to switch me to Geico for 1/3 the price I was paying.  This was before Tesla was even selling cars.

author: @Geckogold
text:
And if that bothers you that much, you can likely get an 18 inch aftermarket wheel for it to regain some if not most of that range back.

But in my experience with my Model Y, long distance travel has gotten a lot easier overall in a Tesla because they keep adding more and more superchargers in many places, so going as far as you absolutely can on one charge is less of an issue than how fast can you charge at each station you do stop at.

Or as Out of Spec Motoring calls it, "supercharger hopping". While you do have to stop more often, your overall trip is usually faster because you're spending less time at said superchargers compared to doing long deep charges at fewer ones that the car tends to do if you don't want to optimize the trip speed.

At one stop, it told me to deep charge for about 40 minutes to make it to the next supercharger which was about two hours away. If I was eating at a restaurant, that might've been fine. But since it was the middle of the night, I instead picked the next supercharger in between where I was charging and where the car wanted me to go. I only had to charge another 5 minutes to make it to the next one, then stopped at that one for maybe 15 minutes, compared to if I did the 40 minutes it originally wanted me to do.

This doesn't always work of course, because if the supercharger is full or you're at a V1/V2 supercharger, you'll probably have to wait. Should also be interesting as more non-Tesla EVs are able to use the V3/V4 superchargers and how they'll impact Tesla owners.
